analysis.one_liner: Shields retailers and distributors from product liability lawsuits unless they made or altered the product.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee without a hearing or vote in the 111th Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: Today, someone hurt by a defective product can sue the store that sold it, not just the manufacturer — a rule that matters most when the maker is hard to find, insolvent, or overseas. This bill would change that: a seller could be sued only if the buyer proved the seller manufactured, designed, installed, or modified the product, and even then only for negligence and only for damages the seller directly caused.
analysis.who_benefits: Retailers, wholesalers, distributors, and other product sellers gain broad immunity from product liability suits, cutting their litigation exposure and insurance costs. Product-liability insurers also gain as claims against sellers shrink.

how_it_helps.text: Exempts lawful sellers from liability for personal injury, monetary loss, or property damage arising from products they sold, unless the claimant proves the seller manufactured, designed, installed, or altered the product [S2][S3].

Even where a seller did one of those non-sale activities, liability would require proof of negligence and be limited to damage directly caused by that activity — a shift from the broader accountability sellers face under product liability law [S2][S3].

The bill's findings state that sellers face increased litigation and insurance costs from being brought into lawsuits over conduct unrelated to the accident, and that limiting their liability would lessen burdens on interstate commerce [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Consumers injured by defective products would lose a legal path against the seller, which often is the easiest defendant to find and sue — particularly when the manufacturer is insolvent, judgment-proof, or located abroad. They would carry more of the risk of products they buy.

drawbacks.text: Injured consumers lose recourse against the seller, who is often the accessible 'deep pocket' defendant when the manufacturer is insolvent, unidentifiable, or out of the country; the bill leaves no alternative channel for those cases [S2][S3].

Where a seller did participate in design, installation, or modification, the bill weakens the standard of accountability from strict product liability to ordinary negligence and caps damages at what the seller's own act directly caused [S2][S3].

The threat of being named in a lawsuit is part of what pressures sellers to stock and sell safe products; removing that exposure could reduce the private enforcement that product liability law currently provides.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Sellers gain real protection from being dragged into suits over products they neither made nor touched, and that has legitimate value. But the bill pays for it entirely with injured consumers' rights: the seller is typically the defendant a consumer can actually reach, and the bill offers no replacement for that recourse when a manufacturer cannot be pursued. It is a clean transfer of risk from commerce to consumers.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Judiciary and Energy and Commerce Committees, sent to a subcommittee, and never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Dan Boren introduced the bill on May 20, 2009, with five original cosponsors, all Republicans [S3].
It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and, in addition, to the House Energy and Commerce Committee [S1][S5].
The next day it was referred to the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Commerce, Trade and Consumer Protection, and no further action was ever recorded [S5].
The bill accumulated 9 cosponsors, all Republicans, and died at the end of the 111th Congress without any vote in either chamber [S4][S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Consumers keep their ability to sue product sellers under existing liability law. Sellers and their insurers gained nothing, since no protection was enacted.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Injured consumers, who keep recourse against sellers

for.name: Rep. Dan Boren
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to limit product sellers' liability, citing unfair costs to sellers from litigation [S3].

for.name: 9 of 179 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; the bill had no Democratic cosponsors beyond its sponsor [S4].

against.name: House Judiciary Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Took no action after referral; the bill sat in committee for the rest of the Congress with no hearing or vote [S5].

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to a consumer protection subcommittee, where it received no further action [S5].

sides.party_line_note: A Democratic sponsor was joined by nine Republican cosponsors and no other Democrats; the bill never advanced far enough for a partisan floor fight.

industries.note: Sellers would gain near-total immunity from product liability suits over products they merely sold, cutting litigation and insurance costs at the direct expense of consumers' ability to recover from an accessible defendant.
Fewer claims against sellers means less exposure for insurers who cover retail and distribution liability.
Lawyers representing injured consumers would lose a major category of viable defendants, shrinking the private enforcement of product safety through the courts.
Manufacturers remain the primary target of suits, but they lose the practical benefit of sellers sharing or shouldering judgments when the manufacturer itself cannot fully pay.
